project.name: phuquoc
project.description: Pho Group Phú Quốc is a comprehensive tourism platform for Phú Quốc island, combining three business modules (PhoFood, Pho Retreat, Pho Travel) with an admin CMS for managing content, bookings, and customers.

nodes.name: page.tsx

nodes.name: website.tsx

nodes.name: DEMO_KHACH_HANG.md

nodes.name: LAYOUT_COMPONENTS.md
nodes.summary: Documentation for the project's layout components (ActivityDetailLayout, HotelDetailLayout, DestinationLayout) and shared components (ImageGallery, BookingForm), including proposed folder structure, usage examples, and dependencies.

nodes.name: README.md
nodes.summary: Project README containing the same detailed customer demo guide as DEMO_KHACH_HANG.md — an overview of the Pho Group Phú Quốc tourism ecosystem, its customer-facing sites, admin system, feature highlights, tech stack, and roadmap.

nodes.languageNotes: Uses ESLint's FlatCompat shim to bridge legacy 'extends'-style shareable configs into the new flat-config format.

nodes.name: next.config.ts

tour.title: What This Project Is
tour.description: Start with the README and the customer demo guide, both written in Vietnamese for stakeholder handover. They frame the Pho Group Phu Quoc platform as one Next.js site serving three customer-facing business modules — PhoFood (seafood and specialty products), Pho Retreat (villa lodging) and Pho Travel (tours and experiences) — plus an admin back office. Read these first so the folder names you meet later map onto real business lines rather than arbitrary route slugs.

tour.title: How a Request Finds Its Locale
tour.description: Every URL on this site is locale-prefixed (/vi/... or /en/...), and two pieces enforce that before any page renders. The edge middleware intercepts unprefixed requests and redirects them to a locale chosen from the Accept-Language header, skipping static assets and API routes; the root page.tsx is a client-side fallback that detects the browser language and redirects while showing a spinner. Understanding this handshake is the prerequisite for everything else — it explains why almost all real pages live under src/app/[locale]/.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js middleware runs on the Edge runtime before routing resolves, so it can rewrite or redirect a request without ever mounting a React tree. Its `matcher` config must explicitly exclude _next/static and image paths, otherwise every asset request pays the middleware cost.

tour.title: The Translation Layer
tour.description: With the locale decided, something has to supply the actual strings. src/i18n.ts is the central configuration declaring supported locales, the default, and the translation dictionary, while en.json and vi.json are key-for-key mirrored catalogues covering common UI, navigation, homepage sections, the 404 screen and the three business lines. Because the catalogues are structurally identical, adding a language is a matter of copying one file and translating values — no code change required.
tour.languageLesson: JSON translation catalogues gain a lot from nesting by feature (common, nav, sections) rather than flat keys — it makes missing-key diffs between locales readable, and lets TypeScript infer the key shape from one catalogue so the others are checked against it.

tour.title: Language State in React
tour.description: LanguageContext is the single most depended-upon module in the codebase — it has the highest fan-in of any node, pulled in by pages and components alike. It exposes the current locale, a setter, the active dictionary from Step 3, and a toggle, all reached through the useLanguage hook. This is the seam where the routing-level locale from Step 2 becomes ordinary React state that any component can read.
tour.languageLesson: React Context is the right tool for low-frequency, widely-read values like locale or theme. Because every consumer re-renders when the provider value changes, a context that changes on every keystroke would be a performance problem — one that changes only on a language toggle is ideal.

tour.title: The App Shell
tour.description: Two nested layouts wrap every page. The root layout owns site-wide SEO metadata (OpenGraph, Twitter cards, robots), loads the Inter font with both Latin and Vietnamese subsets, and injects the Google Analytics and Search Console scripts. The locale layout beneath it generates per-locale metadata and static params, then composes the Header, Footer and FloatingChat shell around page content — this is the tightest cluster in the graph, with Header and Footer both reaching back into the LanguageContext from Step 4.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router nests layouts by directory: the root layout renders once and persists across navigations, while [locale]/layout.tsx re-renders per locale segment. `generateStaticParams` in the locale layout is what lets Next pre-render /vi and /en variants at build time instead of resolving them per request.

tour.title: The Component Library
tour.description: All shared UI lives in src/app/components and is re-exported through a single barrel index.ts, which is why that file ranks near the top for fan-out and is imported by nearly every route. The barrel covers the public site sections plus two sub-families: layouts/ (ActivityDetail, Destination, HotelDetail) and shared/ (BookingForm, ImageGallery). Crucially, the dependency direction is strictly one-way — pages import components, and components never import pages back.
tour.languageLesson: A barrel file (`export * from './X'`) gives consumers one import path and hides internal file organization, so components can be moved without touching callers. The trade-off is bundler work: without `optimizePackageImports` or good tree-shaking, importing one symbol can pull the whole barrel into the bundle.

tour.title: The Data Layer Is Mock
tour.description: There is no backend. src/app/lib/data.ts is the central static module defining the TypeScript interfaces and exporting content for hotels, travel guides, weather, FAQs, footer sections and destinations, while src/mockup/website.tsx supplies Vietnamese activity and destination listings for the homepage carousels. Both rank high in fan-in because pages consume them exactly where API calls would eventually go — the interfaces they define are the contract a real API would have to satisfy.
tour.languageLesson: Declaring interfaces alongside mock data is a useful pre-backend pattern: the type is the API contract, and swapping the hardcoded export for a `fetch` later is a local change because every consumer already codes against the interface, not the literal.

tour.title: The Home Page Composition
tour.description: The locale home page has the highest fan-out in the entire graph — it imports ten section components and composes them into the landing layout: hero, top activities, destinations, transportation, hotels, travel guides, reviews, weather, booking form and FAQ. This is the clearest demonstration of the architecture from Steps 6 and 7 in action, where the page itself holds almost no logic and acts purely as an assembly point over the component library and mock data.

tour.title: The Three Business Modules
tour.description: Each business line from the README gets its own listing route, and all three share the PhoGroupHero component from Step 8 as a common banner and tab bar. PhoFood lists seafood and dried-food products with pricing and shop links, Pho Retreat lists villas with amenities and booking-platform links, and Pho Travel presents tours and cable-car tickets with highlights and ratings. Comparing the three side by side shows the deliberate structural symmetry — same shell, different catalogue.

tour.title: Search, Filter and Sort
tour.description: The Things To Do section is the most stateful part of the public site and forms its own tight cluster in the dependency graph. The page reads filter and sort state from URL search params, applies them to the activities dataset, and renders the filter bar plus a grid of cards; ThingsFilterBar syncs control changes back to the URL through the router, and opens FilterModal for detailed category, price and rating selection. Putting filter state in the URL rather than component state is what makes these views shareable and back-button friendly.
tour.languageLesson: URL search params as the source of truth for filters means the server can read them during render and the browser gets shareable, bookmarkable state for free. The modal still keeps local staging state so the user can adjust several filters before committing one router update, avoiding a navigation per checkbox.

tour.title: Dynamic Detail Pages
tour.description: Booking detail views are dynamic routes: /[locale]/hotels/[id] and /[locale]/1-things-to-do/[id] each look up their record by ID from a colocated mockData file and hand it to a large detail layout component. HotelDetailLayout renders the gallery, tabbed overview/rooms/amenities/location/policies sections, a room booking widget and reviews; ActivityDetailLayout does the equivalent for tours. Both reuse ImageGallery and BookingForm from Step 6, which is exactly why those shared components exist.
tour.languageLesson: `generateStaticParams` on a dynamic segment tells Next.js which [id] values to pre-render at build time. With a fixed mock dataset every detail page becomes static HTML; once a real API arrives you either keep the list small, or switch to on-demand rendering with revalidation.

tour.title: The Admin Back Office
tour.description: The /admin tree is a parallel application with its own layout providing a collapsible sidebar, deliberately bypassed for the login screen. The dashboard shows KPI cards and recent orders, orders management spans bookings and product orders across all three modules, and each business line gets a management screen — Pho Retreat's, for example, edits villa capacity, nightly pricing and availability. Note what is absent: every admin page is 'use client' with hardcoded demo state and no data layer, and login stores a placeholder token in localStorage, so this is a UI prototype rather than a secured system.
tour.languageLesson: A localStorage token with a client-side credential check is authentication theatre — the check runs in the user's own browser and can be edited away. Real protection has to live server-side, in middleware or a route handler, where the client cannot reach it.

tour.title: Styling and Design Tokens
tour.description: Visual consistency comes from two files working together. globals.css imports Tailwind and defines the Pho Group brand color scale plus shared utilities such as the skeleton shimmer, no-scrollbar, sticky tab and filter bars used by the Things To Do page from Step 10, and smooth-scroll offsets. tailwind.config.js extends the theme with the brand blue palette, the Inter font variable loaded by the root layout in Step 5, a soft shadow and the fadeInUp/slideUp animations.
tour.languageLesson: Tailwind's `theme.extend` adds to the default scale rather than replacing it, so brand tokens sit alongside the built-ins. Defining a color once in config and referencing it as a utility class everywhere is what keeps a design system from drifting into one-off hex values scattered through JSX.

tour.title: Analytics and Tracking
tour.description: The one genuine utility module wraps Google Analytics gtag, exposing pageview and event helpers plus domain-specific trackers for bookings, searches and language switches — the last of which pairs directly with the toggle from Step 4. The gtag script itself is injected by the root layout, so this module assumes that global exists. Isolating vendor calls behind named domain functions means swapping analytics providers touches one file instead of every call site.

tour.title: Build Configuration
tour.description: Closing the loop, package.json pins the stack the whole tour has been built on: Next.js 15, React 19, next-intl, Tailwind CSS 4 and lucide-react, with the dev/build/start/lint scripts. next.config.ts whitelists remote images from Unsplash and enables optimized package imports for @heroicons/react, which mitigates the barrel-file bundling trade-off noted in Step 6. tsconfig.json and the ESLint flat config complete the tooling — together these define how everything you have read gets compiled and shipped.
tour.languageLesson: `optimizePackageImports` rewrites barrel imports from large icon and component libraries into deep per-module imports at build time, so importing three icons does not pull in a thousand. Next's `images.remotePatterns` is a security boundary, not a convenience — the image optimizer will refuse any host not listed there.
